newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Scottish business concerned by Tartan Tax.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Scottish business concerned by Tartan Tax.

text.p: For the middle to Plc sized company in Scotland, the implications of devolution and any so-called Tartan Tax remain far from clear.
Some see huge problems for the local economy, others few. But a lack of detail is casting a cloud over the business community.
"Many uncertainties remain to be resolved," says Sir Bruce Pattullo, governor (head) of the Bank of Scotland, one of Scotland's major clearing banks.

The new Labour administration plans a two-question referendum on the future shape of government in Scotland in around three months and a policy document on Scotland is due out at the end of this month.

The referendum will ask Scottish voters to vote "Yes" or "No" to the establishment of a parliament in Edinburgh. It will also ask for a decision on whether such a newly constituted institution should be endowed with tax-varying powers.

It is the second question which is worrying Scottish business and the Scottish arm of the employers' umbrella group, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), has called on the government to scrap the Tartan Tax proposals.
The CBI highlights practical difficulties and costs associated with revenue collection and says that greater democratic powers can be achieved for Scots without additional taxing powers.

"The best outcome would be if the idea was dropped," says Iain McMillan, the CBI's Scottish Director. "At the very least we propose that taxation of small incorporated businesses and business rates are excluded from the parliament's powers."
TAX-VARYING POWERS A HEADACHE FOR LABOUR
The parliament's tax-varying powers provided Labour leader Tony Blair with one of his few headaches during the campaign for the May 1 election.

He vowed that any Labour government would not raise personal income taxes for two years but opponents questioned how this could fit with his proposal for an Edinburgh parliament with tax-varying powers. Was it going to be a toothless tiger, they asked.
Blair did not satisfactorily solve the conundrum but one economic think-tank in Scotland thinks corporate opposition to any business Tartan Tax is a vast over-reaction.
Fraser of Allander Institute has published research which shows that tax-raising powers would not necessarily damage the Scottish economy and could even benefit it.
"Even in the worst likely scenario, the adverse macro-economic impact is relatively small and spread over a considerable time period," said institute director Peter McGregor.

CBI Scotland says these claims are too narrow in perspective but party economist Andrew Wilson cites the Scottish Nationalist Party case that the Tartan Tax is a red herring in the devolution argument.
A three pence in the pound ($5.05) tax-raising power added up to 450 million pounds while Scotland already received 14 billion pounds in grants from central government.
"Instead, a Scottish parliament should be properly devolved and democratically accountable with real economic powers and in charge of all revenues raised from Scotland," Wilson said.
Edinburgh could then send a proportion to the London Treasury, to pay for defence, foreign affairs and other functions where responsibility rested with Westminster.
While not wishing to be seen to be influencing voters, Pattullo urges caution over giving any parliament tax-varying powers.
Once any tax-raising parliament was established, it would probably have to switch focus later on to some form of tax on goods and services, or an additional sales tax, he said.
And any change in taxation would not only handicap business but would also discourage investment in Scotland, Pattullo said.
INVESTMENT
Inward investment to Scotland stands at record levels currently. In the year to end-March 1997, 86 projects worth 3.12 billion pounds had created or safeguarded 14,000 jobs.
Brian Wilson, industry minister for Scotland, points out that since the election, further new investments have occurred despite the prospect of constitutional change.

Bausch and Lomb, the eyecare company, has announced an expansion in Scotland involving 500 jobs. Hyundai Corp, which recently selected Fife for a new 2.4 billion pound semi-conductor plant, is reported by local media to be considering locating a 3,000-job factory in Scotland.
But caution remains, with many business leaders questioning the entire concept of constitutional change.
"What really bothers me is the aggravation it (a parliament) could cause between Scotland and Westminster," said Lord Weir, chairman of the Glasgow-based Weir Group Plc.
Bill Anderson, representing small businesses in Scotland, believes devolution offers an opportunity, not a threat, but agrees that this is very much a small business perspective.

"It is true that a business view could be different depending on size. A small to medium sized concern might not be as worried about the tax question as a middle to bigger sized business," he admits. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
